opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea is pretty simple, even if making it work is hard. For a long time, most of mechanistic interpretability focused on activations. You look at what's happening inside the network as it processes some input, the neurons or directions in activation space, and try to find meaningful features there. Sparse autoencoders are the main example. That's been really productive, but it has some basic limitations. You're describing the network's representations, not quite the computations that produce them. And you're often training a separate model whose reconstructions don't fully match what the original network is actually doing.

Parameter decomposition flips that around. Instead of decomposing activations, we decompose the weights themselves. The network's parameters are where everything it has learned is actually stored, so we ask: can we break the parameter vector into a sum of components, where each component corresponds to one mechanism the network uses?

We want those components to have a few properties. First, they should be faithful: add them all up and you get back the original weights exactly, or very nearly. Second, they should be minimal, meaning that on any given input only a small number of components are needed to reproduce the network's behavior. You can ablate everything else and the output barely changes. And third, they should be simple, so each component uses as little of the network's capacity as possible, for example spanning only a low-rank part of a weight matrix.

If you can find a decomposition like that, you get something quite nice. Each component is a piece of the actual model, not a proxy for it, and it's naturally tied to computation. It tells you "this is the bit of the weights that implements this particular thing," and which inputs cause that bit to get used.

Our first version, Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition, showed this could work on toy models where we knew the ground-truth mechanisms, like toy models of superposition and compressed computation. But it was expensive and fiddly with hyperparameters. Stochastic Parameter Decomposition improved a lot of that. We learn for each component how much it can be ablated on a given input and train with stochastic masking, which makes it more scalable and more robust.

So the bigger picture, for me, is that parameter decomposition is an attempt to get at the network's mechanisms directly, in the space where they actually live. If it scales, I think it can address some conceptual problems the activation-based approach has struggled with, like feature splitting, how to handle computation spread across layers, and how to be sure your explanation reflects what the model is really doing.

r001.rationale: It explicitly contrasts decomposing activations with decomposing the network’s weights.

r002.rationale: It says learned information is stored in the parameters, but does not identify architecture and nonlinearities as jointly implementing the learned algorithm.

r003.rationale: It says components are used on particular inputs and that only a small subset may be needed for a given input.

r004.rationale: It describes components as mechanisms, each implementing a particular thing the network does.

r005.rationale: It does not describe visual features progressing from low-level to higher-order features across layers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, parameter decomposition starts from a slightly different question than most interpretability work. A lot of the field has been asking "what are the representations?" — what directions in activation space mean something — and that's given us sparse autoencoders, probing, all of that. Parameter decomposition asks instead, "what are the mechanisms?" The activations are what the network computes on a particular input, but the parameters are what the network actually learned. They're the thing that's constant across inputs. So if you want to understand what the network has learned, in some sense the parameters are the more fundamental object.

The core idea is to take the network's weights and decompose them into a sum of components, where each component is itself a set of parameters — a vector in parameter space — and the hope is that each one corresponds to some meaningful piece of computation. And then the trick is to pick the decomposition according to some principles that make those pieces interpretable.

The three properties we care about are roughly these. First, faithfulness: if you add all the components back together, you should get the original parameters. We don't want to be describing some other network. Second, minimality: for any given input, the network should only need a small number of the components to reproduce its behaviour on that input. That's the analog of sparsity in SAEs, but at the level of mechanisms rather than features. And third, simplicity: each component should be as simple as possible — for instance, low rank, or spread across as few layers as it needs to be. Without that last constraint, you could trivially satisfy the first two by just making one giant component that is the whole network.

The reason I find this appealing is that it lets you sidestep some of the problems that have been dogging the activation-based approaches. With SAEs, you learn a dictionary that depends heavily on the data distribution you train it on, you get feature splitting, you get features that don't obviously correspond to anything the model is doing mechanistically. Whereas if you decompose the parameters, you're working with the object that actually implements the computation, so the components are mechanisms more or less by construction. You can ask things like, "which of these parameter components was involved in producing this output?" and attribute behaviour directly to them.

I should be honest that this is still early. The methods we've put out — attribution-based parameter decomposition and then the stochastic version that followed — work well on toy models where we know the ground truth, things like toy models of superposition or compressed computation, and they recover the mechanisms we expect. Scaling to real language models is where it gets hard, both computationally and because the optimisation is finicky. But I think the framing is right, and the fact that it connects to a lot of older ideas — things like network pruning, the lottery ticket literature, even some of the singular learning theory work — makes me think we're pointing at something real about how networks organise what they've learned.

r001.rationale: It contrasts activation-based work with decomposing the network’s weights into parameter components.

r002.rationale: It calls parameters what the network learned, but does not say that parameters, architecture, and nonlinearities jointly implement a learned algorithm.

r003.rationale: It says each input may need only a small number of components, but does not state that different inputs can recruit different subsets.

r004.rationale: It describes decomposing weights into components that correspond to meaningful pieces of computation or mechanisms.

r005.rationale: It does not describe visual feature representations progressing from low-level to higher-order features across layers.

astra-6.text:
I think of parameter decomposition as trying to understand a neural network by breaking its weights into meaningful components. The network’s learned knowledge is encoded in its parameters, but it’s not necessarily organized in a way that makes individual neurons or individual weights easy to interpret. A single parameter might participate in lots of different computations.

So the question is: can we find components that are distributed across those parameters, but that each correspond to a more coherent piece of computation? Conceptually, you’re expressing the original weights as a sum of components and trying to find a decomposition that helps explain what the network does.

That’s a slightly different starting point from looking for features in activations. With activations, you’re asking, ‘What information is represented when the model processes this input?’ With parameter decomposition, you’re asking, ‘What learned machinery produces and transforms those representations?’ Those approaches can complement each other.

The hard part is that there are many mathematically valid ways to decompose a set of weights. Simply finding a decomposition doesn’t mean you’ve found the model’s actual computational structure. You want evidence that a component behaves coherently across inputs, and that intervening on it changes the model’s behavior in the way your interpretation predicts. That’s what would turn a convenient description of the weights into a useful explanation of what the network has learned.

r001.rationale: It contrasts decomposing network weights with analyzing information in activations, distinguishing parameters from intermediate activations.

r002.rationale: It describes weights as learned machinery but does not identify parameters, architecture, and nonlinearities together as implementing the learned algorithm.

r003.rationale: It says a parameter may participate in many computations, but does not state that different inputs recruit different subsets of parameters.

r004.rationale: It describes decomposing weights into components that correspond to coherent pieces of computation.

r005.rationale: It does not describe visual features progressing from low-level to higher-order representations across layers.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is to try to understand what a neural network has learned by decomposing its parameters into more interpretable pieces. The weights contain the learned structure of the model, but that structure isn’t necessarily organized in a way where you can point to one neuron or one matrix entry and say, “That’s a particular concept or computation.” It can be distributed across lots of parameters.

So you look for a collection of components that, when added together, reconstruct the model’s weights, and you try to make those components individually meaningful. Ideally, each component corresponds to some relatively coherent part of the model’s computation.

A useful distinction is with approaches that decompose activations. There, you’re asking, “What features are represented when the model processes an input?” With parameter decomposition, you’re asking, “What learned machinery produces and transforms those representations?” Those are complementary questions.

Of course, you can decompose a matrix in many different ways. The hard part is finding a decomposition that actually explains the network. You’d want to test that by intervening on the components and seeing whether the model’s behavior changes in the way your interpretation predicts.

r001.rationale: It contrasts decomposing model weights with decomposing activations produced when processing an input.

r002.rationale: It discusses learned structure in weights, but does not identify parameters, architecture, and nonlinearities together as implementing the learned algorithm.

r003.rationale: It does not state that different inputs can recruit different subsets of parameters.

r004.rationale: It describes decomposing weights into individually meaningful components, ideally corresponding to coherent parts of the model’s computation.

r005.rationale: It does not describe visual features progressing from low-level to higher-order features across layers.
